source_text: Καὶ ἐποίησεν Ἐφὼδ καὶ Θεραφείν. Ἐφὼδ ὕφασμα ἦν ἱερατικὸν, ὅπερ περικειμένῳ τῷ ἱερεῖ ἐφοίτα τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ἡ χάρις. Τὸ δὲ Θεραφεὶν τοιοῦτο μέντοι, οὐ θεῖκὸν δὲ, ἀλλʼ εἰδωλικὸν, ὡς ἐν ταῖς βασιλείαις δείκνυται.
thought_title: The ephod and the household idol
orientation: Origen is explaining the objects mentioned in the story of Micah, distinguishing the priestly ephod from the idolatrous theraphin.
pass_a_gloss: And he made [an] ephod and [a] theraphin. [The] ephod was [a] woven garment priestly, which [when] worn by the priest, the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon [him]. But the theraphin [was] such indeed, but not divine, but idolatrous, as in the books of Kingdoms it is shown.

choices.why: Glossary term; renders the idolatrous object as distinct from the divine ephod.
Keeps the noun-adjective order of the source while remaining natural in English.
The verb suggests habitual or repeated coming; 'came upon' preserves the motion toward the priest.
Glossary maps this to the books of Kingdoms; modern readers know them as Samuel and Kings.
Renders the adjective as a quality of the object, contrasting with idolatrous.

pass_b_english: He made an ephod and a household idol. The ephod was a priestly woven garment, and when the priest wore it, the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon him. The household idol, however, was not divine but idolatrous, as is shown in the books of Kingdoms (Samuel and Kings).
